title: Garden Sprinkler
hook: No motor: two jets of water push the arm round, the same way a rocket flies.
summary: A sprinkler has to spread water over a lawn evenly, using nothing but the pressure in the hose. This one does it with no motor at all: the water leaving the arm pushes it round.

Water from the hose comes up a column in the middle of the wheeled frame and into the arm through a swivel. At each end of the arm a nozzle points the water outwards, a little up and a little sideways.

Squirting water backwards pushes the nozzle forwards, as a rocket’s exhaust pushes the rocket. On this model the arm turns at about 170 rpm, where the push at 2 bar settles once friction and the water’s own swing have taken their share.

facts.label: Throw
facts.value: about 7 m, a circle 14 m across

parts.label: Frame and column
parts.about: The hose screws on at the front. The water turns up the column in the middle to the swivel at its top.

parts.label: Arm
parts.about: Hollow, with its hub on the column. Water pressure lifts the hub onto a washer that seals the joint and takes the arm’s weight as it turns.

parts.label: Left nozzle
parts.about: Points the water outwards, 20° up and a little sideways. The sideways part of the jet is what turns the arm.

parts.label: Right nozzle
parts.about: The same as the left one, pointing the other way round, so the two pushes add up to a turn.

parts.label: Wheels
parts.about: Two wheels at the back, so it can be pulled by the hose to the next patch of lawn.

annotations.title: Nozzles
annotations.text: Each squirts about 5.7 litres a minute at 19 m/s. Pushing the water out backwards pushes the nozzle forwards with about 1.8 newtons: the air plays no part in it.

annotations.title: Swivel
annotations.text: The arm’s hub sits on the column. Water pressure lifts it onto a washer, which seals the joint and makes the face it turns on.

annotations.title: Hose connector
annotations.text: At 3 bar at the tap, about 2 bar is left at the nozzles once the hose, the tap and the swivel have taken their share.

annotations.title: Wheels
annotations.text: Pull it by the hose and it rolls to the next patch, still turning.

how.label: The idea
how.title: Pushed round by its own water
text: Water comes up the column into the arm and leaves through the two nozzles. Each nozzle throws its water outwards and a little sideways, and as it does, the water pushes back on it.
The two pushes point opposite ways at opposite ends of the arm, so together they turn it. Nothing else drives it: no motor, no gears.

how.label: Water in
how.title: Up the column, through the swivel
text: The hose screws on at the front of the frame. The water turns up the column in the middle and into the arm’s hub, which turns on the top of the column.
At 3 bar at the tap, about 2 bar is left by the time the water reaches the nozzles, and the two of them pass about 11 litres a minute.

how.label: The push
how.title: A rocket on a stick
text: A nozzle squirting water backwards is pushed forwards, just as a rocket is pushed by its exhaust: it is the water leaving that pushes, not the water pressing on the air. A sprinkler would turn in a vacuum.
More pressure means faster jets and a harder push, so the arm turns faster and the water goes further. Pick a pressure.

chart.title: How far it throws
chart.caption: From the middle to where 2 mm drops land, in still air.

speeds.label: 1 bar
speeds.note: Jets at 14 m/s, 0.9 N each: the arm turns at about 80 rpm.

speeds.label: 2 bar
speeds.note: Jets at 19 m/s, 1.8 N each: about 170 rpm, water out to 7 m.

speeds.label: 3 bar
speeds.note: Jets at 24 m/s, 2.7 N each: about 220 rpm, water out to nearly 8 m.

how.label: Speed
how.title: Where the push goes
text: Why doesn’t the arm spin faster and faster? Every drop entering at the middle has to be swung out to the tip at the arm’s speed, and that takes most of the push: at 166 rpm about three quarters of it. Friction in the swivel takes most of the rest.

Turned fully sideways, the same nozzles would spin the arm at well over 1,000 rpm, but the faster they move, the more their own speed cancels the jets’ and the water drops short. A slight angle throws further.

chart.title: Where the push goes at 166 rpm
chart.caption: Shares of the jets’ turning push, 0.13 N·m in all.

how.label: Throw
how.title: 20° up and a little to the side
text: Water needs height to travel, so the nozzles tip up 20°. With no air it would carry 25 m; drag on the drops brings it down to about 7 m, a wetted circle 14 m across.
Run backwards, sucking water in, a sprinkler turns the other way, about 40 times slower: a puzzle Feynman posed, settled by experiment in 2024.

chart.title: Turning the nozzles sideways
chart.caption: The more sideways the nozzles point, the faster the arm turns and the shorter the throw (2 bar, 2 mm drops).
